title: /interface/bridge/port/print
task: See which physical ports are members of the bridge
aliases: which ports are in the bridge
explain: **A physical port that is not a member of the bridge forms its own private broadcast domain.** DHCP uses broadcast, DNS uses broadcast, and discovery protocols use broadcast — none of them cross a bridge boundary. This is the number one MikroTik beginner fault.
`running` in the print output means the port is enabled in the bridge, not that it has a cable. The physical state is separate.
`pvid` sets the VLAN that untagged traffic on that port belongs to. It matters on a trunk; on an access port it is simply the VLAN that traffic defaults into.
In RouterOS 7 this menu is `/interface/bridge/port`. In v6 it was `/interface bridge port`. If you cannot find it, check your version first.
example: A PC on ether5 gets 169.254.x.x while every other PC works. `/interface/bridge/port/print` shows ether5 has no bridge entry. It is physically up and completely alone.

errors.means: The bridge does not exist under that name. Bridge names are case-sensitive.

errors.message: Adding the port drops your management session
errors.means: You are connected through that port and the bridge has no address or DHCP yet.
errors.fix: Set the bridge IP and DHCP server BEFORE adding the management port, or connect from a different port.

title: /ip/route/print
task: Read the routing table and find how traffic leaves and returns
commands:
/ip/route/print
/ip/route/print where dst-address=0.0.0.0/0
/ip/route/print detail
/ip/route/print where gateway=ether1
/tool/fetch mode=resolve
/ping 1.1.1.1 count=5
/ping example.com count=5
explain: RouterOS does **longest-prefix match** here too. `10.0.0.0/8` and `10.1.0.0/16` both matching means the /16 wins, whatever the distance column says.
Routes marked with `D` are dynamic (from DHCP or PPP). Those come and go with the link — a default route that disappears when the WAN reconnects is usually a dynamic route that was never made static.
**The single most useful test is the pair of pings**: ping an IP address, then ping a name. IP works + name fails = DNS problem. Both fail = routing, NAT or firewall.
Check `gateway=` and `distance=` — a static default route with distance 1 competes with a dynamic one, and the dynamic one often wins unexpectedly.
`/tool/fetch` resolves and downloads in one step and reports the actual nameserver used.
example: Client can ping 1.1.1.1 but cannot resolve anything. Name resolution and routing are separate systems, and this test separates them in one command.

errors.means: DNS is not working, but routing may be perfectly fine.
No reply. Could be routing, NAT, or the upstream blocking ICMP — check in that order.
errors.fix:
/ip/firewall/nat/print   # masquerade must exist on the WAN interface
/ip/firewall/filter/print stats

title: /ip firewall nat
task: Check and set up masquerading and port forwarding
risks: An `action=accept` masquerade with `to-addresses=0.0.0.0` on a wrong interface can expose internal services to the internet. Always specify the out-interface and the internal network.
commands:
/ip/firewall/nat/print
/ip/firewall/nat/add chain=srcnat action=masquerade out-interface=ether1
/ip/firewall/nat/add chain=dstnat protocol=tcp dst-port=443 \
   in-interface=ether1 action=dst-nat to-addresses=10.10.20.20 to-ports=443
/ip/firewall/nat/print stats
explain: Two chains, two purposes. **`srcnat` makes internal clients work outbound** (masquerade). **`dstnat` makes inbound connections reach an internal host** (port forwarding). Forgetting the NAT is why a client can reach the internet but nothing reaches it.
`masquerade` rewrites the source to the outgoing interface address; `src-nat` rewrites it to an address you specify. Use masquerade on dynamic links (pppoe-out, DHCP WAN) and src-nat on static ones.

**The port-forwarding chain is `dstnat` and must be in the `input` chain** for traffic terminating on the router itself, or in `forward` for traffic passing through. Getting the chain wrong is the second most common NAT fault.
RouterOS 7's address-list approach is cleaner than long chain chains: match an address list, apply a rule. For learning the basics the simple form is fine.
Add `stats` when diagnosing — a NAT rule with zero hits is not doing what you think.
example: You add a port forward for an internal web server and nothing happens. `/ip/firewall/nat/print` shows the rule in `forward`, but the destination is this router, which is `input`. Wrong chain.
verify:
/ip/firewall/nat/print stats
# from a machine outside: curl -I http://<public-ip>:<port>

errors.message: Client can get an address but has no internet
errors.means: No working masquerade, or the client's gateway is not this router.
errors.fix:
/ip/firewall/nat/print
Check the client's gateway with ipconfig.

errors.means: Wrong chain, no NAT rule at all, or the ISP is blocking inbound on that port.
errors.fix:
/ip/firewall/nat/print stats  (look for packets on the rule)
Then /ip/firewall/filter/print stats

errors.means: A dynamic default route disappeared after a WAN reconnect, or a dhcp-client lease changed the address.
errors.fix:
/ip/route/print where dynamic
Make the default route static rather than accepting the dynamic one.

title: /system/resource/print
task: Check CPU, memory, uptime and whether the router is struggling
explain: `free-memory` and especially `free-hdd-space` matter more than CPU on most boards. A router that has been up for months accumulates log and database bloat.
High CPU is usually caused by a firewall rule set that scans huge address lists, not by normal forwarding. Look at the counters with `/ip/firewall/filter/print stats`.
**`/system/backup/save` before any configuration change is the single most valuable habit on RouterOS.** It is instant, tiny, and it is the only reliable rollback.
`/system/clock/print` matters more than it looks — certificates, TLS and logging all depend on the clock being right, especially after a router has been unpowered.
example: A router has been up 200 days and clients report intermittent slowness. `free-memory` is low and `/system/backup/save` restores service immediately after a reboot. Backups before changes catch this.

errors.message: Router is unresponsive and WinBox will not connect
errors.means: It may have crashed or run out of memory.
errors.fix: Connect via the serial console. Then /system/backup/load name=<last good> and reboot.

title: /system/backup/save
task: Save a binary configuration backup you can restore
changes: Writes a .backup file to the router's filesystem. Does not change the running configuration.
undo: n/a — a backup does not alter anything
risks: Safe by design. The risk is not taking one.
explain: **`.backup` is binary and complete** — keys, certificates, passwords, everything. **`/export` is a readable `.rsc` text file** that deliberately omits secrets and is the safer thing to share or paste into a ticket.
Take a backup before every change. It costs nothing and it is the only rollback that always works.
To move a config to different hardware, use `/export` and `/import` — a binary backup will not restore onto different hardware or a different RouterOS architecture.
A backup file on the router's flash is lost when you replace the device. Copy it off with `/file/print` then fetch it from a computer.
example: You add a firewall rule over WinBox and lose your session. `/system/backup/load name=before-change` restores the router in seconds. Without that backup you are reading the config out of the terminal by hand.

errors.message: No such file or directory (bad file name)
errors.means: The backup name does not exist — probably a different name than you think.
errors.fix: /system/backup/print   to list what is actually there
